title: Does homefield advantage exist at Nebraska anymore?
text:
We have all heard the passing comments that Memorial stadium became the third largest city in Nebraska on game days, and we all have heard the storied history of Nebraska’s nation leading 416 game sellout streak that dates back to 1961. Blah. Blah. Blah.
Who cares? Does anyone?
The questions that should be asked are; Does it matter? Does the continuation of the sell out streak actually help Nebraska football?
And most importantly, does home-field advantage even exist for Nebraska football anymore? While it seems pretty intuitive that yes, Nebraska will do better at home compared to on the road the data shows an interesting story.
Over the past decade of Nebraska football, fans have been party to some of the most heart breaking and gut wrenching losses and even worse some of those losses have been at Memorial stadium. Does 2025 vs Iowa ring a bell, anyone?
However the data shows that Nebraska football, over the past 10 years at least, is actually more likely to win at home.




Code
library(tidyverse)

Code
library(cfbfastR)
all_pbp <- load_cfb_pbp(seasons = 2016:2025)




Code
Nu <- all_pbp |>
  filter(
    team == "Nebraska"
  )

  nu_scores <- Nu |>
  mutate(
    nebraska_score = case_when(
      pos_team == "Nebraska" ~ pos_team_score,
      def_pos_team == "Nebraska" ~ def_pos_team_score,
      TRUE ~ NA_integer_
    ),
    opponent_final_score = case_when(
      pos_team == "Nebraska" ~ def_pos_team_score,
      def_pos_team == "Nebraska" ~ pos_team_score,
      TRUE ~ NA_integer_
    )
  )

nu_game_results <- nu_scores |>
  group_by(game_id, season, home_team, away_team, neutral_site) |>
  summarise(
    nebraska_score = max(nebraska_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    opponent_final_score = max(opponent_final_score, na.rm = TRUE),
  ) 


`summarise()` has regrouped the output.
ℹ Summaries were computed grouped by game_id, season, home_team, away_team, and
  neutral_site.
ℹ Output is grouped by game_id, season, home_team, and away_team.
ℹ Use `summarise(.groups = "drop_last")` to silence this message.
ℹ Use `summarise(.by = c(game_id, season, home_team, away_team, neutral_site))`
  for per-operation grouping (`?dplyr::dplyr_by`) instead.


Code
  nu_game_locations <- nu_game_results |>
  mutate(
    game_location = case_when(
      home_team == "Nebraska" ~ "Home",
      away_team == "Nebraska" ~ "Away",
      neutral_site == TRUE ~ "Neutral"
    )
  )

  nu_game_records <- nu_game_locations |>
  mutate(
    game_result = case_when(
      nebraska_score > opponent_final_score ~ "Win",
      nebraska_score < opponent_final_score ~ "Loss",
    )
  )

 nu_win_percentage <- nu_game_records |>
  group_by(game_location) |>
  summarise(
    total_games = n(),
    wins = sum(game_result == "Win", na.rm = TRUE),
    losses = sum(game_result == "Loss", na.rm = TRUE),
    winning_percentage = wins / total_games * 100
  ) 




Code
ggplot(nu_win_percentage, aes(x = game_location, y = winning_percentage, fill = game_location)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Home" = "red",
      "Away" = "grey"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Nebraska Football's Home-Field Advantage",
    subtitle = "At home Nebraska is winning 53.7% of games compared to 28% on the road over the last 10 seasons.",
    x = "Game Location",
    y = "Winning Percentage (%)",
    caption = "Source: cfbfastR / SportsDataverse | By: Heath Topil"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 8),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none"
  )









By a wide margin as well, Nebraska has a differential of 25% between home and away winning percentages. Quite shocking when we really sit down and think about Nebraska home games over the last decade.
Additionally, Nebraska has been on a tear scoring points while at Memorial Stadium.


Code
nu_season_points <- nu_game_records |>
  filter(neutral_site == FALSE) |>
  group_by(season, game_location) |>
  summarise(
    average_points_scored = mean(nebraska_score)
  )


`summarise()` has regrouped the output.
ℹ Summaries were computed grouped by season and game_location.
ℹ Output is grouped by season.
ℹ Use `summarise(.groups = "drop_last")` to silence this message.
ℹ Use `summarise(.by = c(season, game_location))` for per-operation grouping
  (`?dplyr::dplyr_by`) instead.




Code
ggplot(nu_season_points, aes(x = season, y = average_points_scored, color = game_location, group = game_location)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Home" = "red",
      "Away" = "grey"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = 2016:2025
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Nebraska's Scoring at Home vs. Away",
    subtitle = "Average points scored per game by season",
    x = "Season",
    y = "Average Points Scored",
    color = "Game Location",
    caption = "Source: cfbfastR | By Heath Topil"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.position = "right"
  )









However, these home games also take into account lesser opponents in the non-conference schedule. Yet, when we look at the graph more closely, we see that only twice in the last 10 seasons Nebraska has scored more on the road compared to at home.
Even more interesting is the fact that, over the last decade, Nebraska football has been averaging just over 28 points a game while at home and 22 when on the road. When looking at Nebraska’s opponents over the last 10 years, they average around 23 points per game when playing at Memorial Stadium. Yet, when Nebraska travels on the road, opponents are averaging just shy of 30 points per game against the Cornhuskers.


Code
nu_location_scoring <- nu_game_records |>
  filter(neutral_site == FALSE) |>
  group_by(game_location) |>
  summarise(
    nebraska_average = mean(nebraska_score),
    opponent_average = mean(opponent_final_score)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(nebraska_average, opponent_average),
    names_to = "team",
    values_to = "average_points"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    team = recode(
      team,
      nebraska_average = "Nebraska",
      opponent_average = "Opponents"
    ),
    game_location = factor(game_location, levels = c("Home", "Away"))
  )




Code
ggplot(nu_location_scoring, aes(x = game_location, y = average_points, group = team, color = team)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Nebraska" = "red",
      "Opponents" = "grey"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Nebraska Football's Home-Field Advantage",
    subtitle = "Average points scored by Nebraska and its opponents, 2016–2025",
    x = "Game Location",
    y = "Average Points Per Game",
    color = "Team",
    caption = "Source: cfbfastR | By Heath Topil"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.position = "right"
  )

So…whats the deal?
What is the answer to the question we started off with? Does homefield advantage even exist for Nebraska football anymore?
The data says yes. Every piece of data shows that Nebraska football wins more games, and scores more points when they are at home. Even more interesting is the fact that it’s not even really close, Nebraska greatly outscores their opponents on average over the last 10 years when playing at Memorial Stadium.
So, despite the fact that Nebraska may appear to be the most cursed college football team in recent memory, the fans need to continue showing up. Because when at home, Nebraska football consistently wins more games.
